title: Responsible AI Frameworks in Practice

thumbnail.headline: Six Questions, Every Time

slide.title: Six Questions, Every Time
slide.body: A stack of thick framework documents on the left; on the right, one small card with six tick boxes. Small tag: AI Ethics, Bias and Safety · Lesson 7.

production_notes: [VERIFY] The OECD AI Principles and the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence are named only as examples of international frameworks, at a high level. Names, dates of adoption and exact wording must be checked against the official sources before recording. The content.md statement that both were agreed by many countries is left out of the voiceover until confirmed.
Scene 3 slide must not quote any framework wording; show the two names only, with no dates or logos.
Katarzyna Nowak and her marketing agency in Poland are fictional; the product, the client and the '40%' energy claim are invented examples of an unchecked AI draft and must be shown struck through.
Legal duties point to AI-30; the voiceover says this in one line only.

Hook.voiceover: Governments, international organisations and companies have written many documents about responsible AI. They have different names and lengths. But read them side by side, and you find the same few ideas again and again. Those ideas can fit on a card on your desk.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we looked at safety and human oversight. Now we bring the course together. A responsible AI framework is a set of principles that describes how AI should be built and used. Some are written by international organisations, some by governments, and many by companies for their own staff.

slide.title: Who writes frameworks?
slide.body: Three sources feeding one 'Principles' box: International organisations · Governments · Companies (for their own staff).

Explain.voiceover: Two well-known international examples come from the OECD and from UNESCO. In this beginner course, we do not study their exact wording. Instead, we look at the ideas that they and many company frameworks share.

slide.title: International examples
slide.body: OECD AI Principles · UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. Caption: we focus on the shared ideas, not the exact wording.

Explain.voiceover: Six core principles appear in most frameworks. Fairness, so AI does not treat people unjustly. Transparency, so people know when AI is used. Privacy, so personal and confidential data is protected. Safety, so AI does not cause harm, and outputs are checked. Accountability, so a named person is responsible. And human oversight, so a capable person can question and change decisions.

slide.title: Six shared principles
slide.body: Fairness · Transparency · Privacy · Safety · Accountability · Human oversight (each with a small icon and the lesson where we met it)

Explain.voiceover: Frameworks can feel far away from daily work. So the practical step is to turn each principle into one question you ask yourself, before, during or after you use an AI tool. That is a responsible-use checklist. It does not replace your organisation's rules. Legal duties are covered in course AI thirty.

slide.title: From principle to question
slide.body: Principle (e.g. Privacy) → arrow → one yes/no question → Responsible-use checklist. Footnote: supports your organisation's rules; legal duties in AI-30.

Explain.voiceover: Before take-off, pilots use a short checklist, even after thousands of flights. It does not teach them to fly. It makes sure they do not forget something important when they are busy. Your checklist does the same for AI. It gives you a few quick questions that stop you from skipping a step on a busy day.
Explain.stock_query: pilot reading preflight checklist in cockpit

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see one in use. Katarzyna Nowak works at a marketing agency in Poland. Her team uses a chatbot to draft social media posts and client reports. After this course, she writes six questions, one for each principle.
Demonstrate.stock_query: marketing team working on social posts

Demonstrate.voiceover: For example. For privacy, have I removed all personal and client-confidential details? For safety, have I checked every fact and number against a trusted source? For fairness, could this output use stereotypes? And for human oversight, did I read and edit the output myself? Transparency and accountability get a question too.

slide.title: Katarzyna's checklist
slide.body: Privacy: personal and client details removed? · Safety: facts and numbers checked? · Fairness: any stereotypes? · Transparency: disclosed where rules require? · Human oversight: did I edit it? · Accountability: who fixes problems?

Demonstrate.voiceover: She uses it on a real task, an AI-drafted post for a client's new product. Her prompt included the client's unreleased price, so she replaces it with a placeholder. The draft claims the product reduces energy use by forty percent. She cannot find this in the client's material, so she deletes it. And the draft shows only young people, so she widens the description.

slide.title: Three problems caught
slide.body: Privacy: unreleased price → placeholder. Safety: '40% less energy' claim, not in client material → struck through. Fairness: only young people shown → wider description.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her agency's rule is to tell clients when AI helped, so she adds a note to her email. She edits the final text herself, and she signs off the post as account manager. The whole checklist takes about five minutes, and it catches three real problems that would otherwise have reached the client.

slide.title: Five minutes, all six checked
slide.body: Transparency: note to client · Human oversight: she edits the text · Accountability: she signs off as account manager

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to read a framework once and file it away. Principles only help if they change what you do, so use your questions every time. Write each question so you can answer yes or no for a real task. And always check official sources before quoting a named framework.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, many international and company frameworks share the same core principles: fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, accountability and human oversight. Second, principles become useful when you turn each one into a short question for a real task. Third, a responsible-use checklist supports, but does not replace, your organisation's rules and the law.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Six shared principles across frameworks. 2. Turn each into a short question. 3. A checklist supports, not replaces, rules and the law.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will build your own six-question checklist and use it on one real task you did with an AI tool this month. Keep it, because you will use it again in your capstone audit. In the next lesson, we will start that capstone by testing an AI tool for bias. See you there.
